---
title: "Precision with Runs"
description: "The same guard two ways — recall vs precision."
---

Page one's token list lowers to `Runs`, which matches the parsed argv of each command in the line. The other spelling, `block_command(r"git\s+stash", ...)`, keeps a regex over the raw text. That reach is what lets a pattern span a pipe, a redirect, or a flag's value, and it is also what makes this one block `git commit -m "git stash"` — a command you actually want to run. Same input, two verdicts, side by side:

<!-- gd-embed-widget: runs_guard -->

Work through the presets and watch the verdicts split. The table shows what the real engine answers — Pattern is the string spelling, `Runs` is the token spelling page one used, and the widget runs the `Runs` version (it declines wrapper payloads honestly; `capt-hook test` covers those for real):

| Command | Pattern | `Runs` |
|---|---|---|
| `git stash` | blocks | blocks |
| `git commit -m "git stash"` | blocks | allows — it's an argument, not a command |
| `echo "git stash"` | blocks | allows |
| `sudo git stash` | blocks | **allows** — `Runs` sees `sudo`'s argv, not what it wraps |
| `sh -c "git stash"` | blocks | **blocks** — the parser descends into the payload |

The last two rows are the lesson, and they cut in opposite directions. `Runs` matches structure, so a wrapper like `sudo` hides the command from it — cover wrappers with their own entry. But a string payload doesn't hide anything: the parser descends into `sh -c` and finds the `git stash` inside. Precision costs you wrappers, not depth.

So pick by shape, not by nerve. Tokens when you mean a command: `block_command(["rm", "-rf"], ...)` names one, and a line that only quotes the words never trips it. A string when you mean text no argv prefix names — `block_command(r"curl.*\|\s*sh", ...)` guards a pipeline, which no token list can describe.
